lines.text: In Lebanon's Bekaa valley there is a wall with three stones in it. Each one is about nineteen metres long, and each one weighs roughly as much as two fully loaded jumbo jets.
They are called the Trilithon. Two thousand years ago somebody cut them, moved them, and laid them side by side so neatly you can barely slide a blade between them.
Online the answer is simple. Nobody in the ancient world could move eight hundred tons. So the platform must be older than history: a landing pad, built by visitors from somewhere else.
So let's treat it like a real job. Imagine we run a heavy-haulage firm, and a client hands us that brief: move the Trilithon, using only what existed back then. Can we quote it?
Eight line items. Each one tests a claim. At the end, we add up the invoice and deliver a verdict. If the job is impossible, the quote will tell us.

ch: WHAT ARE WE MOVING, AND WHERE

lines.text: Line one: the site survey. Baalbek sits near the top of the Bekaa valley, by springs that water the plain. Archaeologists have found that the hill was lived on since the Neolithic.
The Greeks and Romans called the town Heliopolis, the city of the sun. On top of the old hill the Romans raised a sanctuary to Jupiter, with columns about twenty metres tall. Six still stand.
Next door is the so-called Temple of Bacchus, one of the best preserved Roman temples anywhere. UNESCO lists the whole site as a World Heritage property.
Our load sits in the western wall of the temple podium. Not under the temple, notice. In the wall that holds the hill up on its steep side.
That detail matters. The giant blocks appear where the ground falls away. A retaining wall works better the heavier and more solid its stones are. Big stones there are engineering, not decoration.
The landing-pad story pictures a flat runway of giant slabs. Our survey finds something else: a temple platform with the biggest blocks only along one slope.
So the survey is done. We know what the stones do and where they sit. Now we need to know exactly how heavy they are.
Line two: the load. Each Trilithon block is about nineteen metres long, four point two metres high and three point six metres deep.

Let's do the maths ourselves. That's about two hundred and eighty-seven cubic metres of limestone. At roughly two point seven tonnes per cubic metre, we get about seven hundred and seventy-five tonnes.

That matches the published estimates of seven hundred and fifty to eight hundred tonnes. The course underneath holds blocks of around three hundred tonnes or more. Big, but each one is a known number.
Now compare the client brief. Erich von Däniken wrote that some blocks weigh nearly two thousand tons. No surveyed block at Baalbek is that heavy, not even the biggest one still in the quarry.
Weights grow in the retelling. Eight hundred becomes a thousand, a thousand becomes two thousand. On our quote we write what the measurements say: about eight hundred per block.
Is eight hundred tonnes a lot? Absolutely. These are among the heaviest stones ever placed in a building. That is the honest part of the mystery, and we keep it.
So the load is real, and it is huge. Next question: where did it come from, and how do you cut something that size out of a hill?

ch: THE QUARRY THAT KEPT ITS SECRETS

lines.text: Line three: the cut. The source is no secret. About eight hundred to nine hundred metres from the temple lies the ancient quarry, and the stones are still there.
The most famous is the Stone of the Pregnant Woman, roughly twenty metres long and about a thousand tonnes. It lies tilted, half freed, still joined to the bedrock at its base.
Unfinished blocks are a gift. They show the method in mid-step. Narrow channels were cut around the block, and the stone was split along natural layers in the rock.
The German Archaeological Institute's quarry team compares it to how Roman masons cut stone elsewhere: split from the bedrock along the natural fissures, then trimmed to shape.

In twenty fourteen that team, with Jeanine Abdul Massih of the Lebanese University, dug around the Pregnant Woman to study the cutting and transport. They documented tool marks and searched the old spoil heaps for datable pottery.
The brief says lasers. But a laser leaves smooth melted faces, not chisel grooves. What the quarry shows is iron tools, wedges and patience.
So we can quote the cut: a quarry crew, iron tools, and months of work per block. Hard, slow, expensive. Not mysterious. The real question is the next line.
Line four: the route. Any hauler asks this first. Is it uphill? Here is the good news for the Romans: the quarry is slightly higher than the temple platform.

Researchers who studied the ground, from Jean-Pierre Adam in the nineteen seventies onward, point out that a block could travel from quarry to wall on a level or gently falling road, without ever being lifted.
That changes the whole job. You don't need to raise eight hundred tonnes into the sky. You need to drag it across less than a kilometre of prepared, level track.
Adam also noticed that the unfinished blocks sit raised and tilted in their pits. That leaves room to slide timber underneath as the block is freed, so it can end up on rollers without being lifted.
The brief imagines anti-gravity because it assumes the stones had to fly. The route says they only had to slide.
Distance, under a kilometre. Gradient, slightly downhill. Now the expensive line: the crew and the gear.
Line five: crew and gear. The key machine is the capstan: a vertical drum with long bars. People walk in a circle, and the drum winds a rope with many times their pulling force.

Chain several capstans together, anchor them in the ground ahead of the block, and pull. Margarete van Ess of the German institute named the capstan as the most likely method, with sledges also under discussion.

How many people? An old estimate claimed forty thousand men for the Pregnant Woman. Jean-Pierre Adam worked through the mechanics and arrived at a far smaller crew: on the order of one hundred and forty-four, working capstans.

Too optimistic? We have a test case. In seventeen sixty-nine and seventy, the Russians moved the Thunder Stone, a granite boulder of well over a thousand tonnes, to become the base of Peter the Great's statue.

They used no animals and no engines. Around four hundred men dragged it on a sledge riding over bronze balls in grooved tracks, about six kilometres overland, roughly two hundred metres on a good day.
That stone was heavier than any Trilithon block, and its route was longer. The job was done with human muscle in the age of candles.

And the Romans had their own heavy kit: treadwheel cranes, compound pulleys and capstans, shown on monuments and described by engineers like Vitruvius. They lifted column parts weighing many tonnes at Baalbek itself.
So line five comes out at hundreds of workers, not tens of thousands. Expensive, organised, imperial. No visitors required.
Line six: the placement. Here is a clue on the stones themselves. Many Roman blocks carry lifting holes for iron grips. The Trilithon blocks show no visible lifting sockets on top.
That fits the route. If the lower courses were built first and earth was banked up behind and in front of them, the big block could be slid along at ground level, straight onto its course.
Then the final centimetres: levers, wedges and patience, nudging it into place until the joint closes. Afterwards the temporary earth comes away, and the stone appears to float above the ground.
The tight joints impress everyone. But the same precision is found across Roman architecture. Fine joints are a sign of skilled masons, not of alien machines.
The brief says the blocks were levitated into place. The stones themselves say they were slid. No lifting holes, a level road, and a wall built from the ground up.
So the haul and the placement are quotable. Now the paperwork. When was this job actually done, and for whom?
Line seven: the paperwork. Every job leaves records. The brief says the platform is tens of thousands of years old. The site disagrees.
First clue: researchers reported part of a Roman column drum under the course that carries the Trilithon. Whatever lies under a stone was there before the stone was laid.

Second clue: a Roman architect's sketch of the temple's gable, engraved on top of one of the Trilithon blocks. Some scholars say a sketch alone can't date the stone. Taken with the rest, it points the same way.
Third: a graffito on one of the top column drums shows the Temple of Jupiter was standing almost to its capitals by around AD sixty, in the reign of Nero.
And there is an older layer. German researchers found that a large pre-Roman terrace stood here first and was never finished. The Roman podium was wrapped around it in the first century AD.
Margarete van Ess sums it up: the Temple of Jupiter was definitely built by the Romans, in at least four phases, from around fifteen BC into the early third century AD.

So where did the landing pad come from? In nineteen fifty-nine a Soviet mathematician, Matest Agrest, suggested the terrace was a launch site. Zecharia Sitchin later claimed the Epic of Gilgamesh describes rockets at a Landing Place here.
But researchers who checked point out that the Epic of Gilgamesh contains no rocket launch and no Landing Place. The paperwork for the alien theory is from the twentieth century.
Line eight: the abandoned loads. Every big job has a pile of things that went wrong. At Baalbek, they are the most impressive stones of all.
The German team found why the Pregnant Woman stayed put. At one edge the stone quality was poor. It could have broken in transport. So they left a thousand tonnes where it lay.

And right beside it, in twenty fourteen, they found another. About nineteen point six metres long, six wide, at least five and a half high: roughly one thousand six hundred and fifty tonnes, the largest worked stone block known from antiquity.
Local legends filled the gap long before aliens did. Giants built it for Nimrod. Solomon built it with spirits, and the blocks were left in the quarry because the spirits went on strike.
The stone's own name comes from a story: a pregnant woman promised to reveal how to move it, if the townspeople fed her until she gave birth. She never revealed a thing.
The true open question is why so big. Van Ess says the podium stones are bigger than they need to be. Her institute studies exactly that: projects built to impress, at the edge of what was possible.
The final invoice. Let's add up every line of the quote.

A quarry under a kilometre away, with matching blocks: evidence. A route that never goes uphill: evidence. Roman dating from the drum, the sketch and the AD sixty graffito: evidence. Capstans and rollers with hundreds of workers: plausible.
An alien landing pad: no evidence. Two thousand tons and tens of thousands of years: inflated. The exact haulage method, and why the stones are so oversized: still open.
The verdict. The Trilithon was moved by Roman builders in the first century AD, from a quarry just up the road, on a route that never climbed, with capstans, rollers and a great many hands.
The job was real, and it was close to the limit of the ancient world. Just not past it. In seventeen seventy another crew moved an even heavier stone with nothing but muscle.
What stays open is human: why one city wanted stones this big, and why they stopped. The quarry still holds the answer, under a few more metres of earth.
If you ran the haulage firm, what would you charge for this job? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
